tier_reason: Upgraded from D. Bitcoin Core PR #6954, which switched validation from OpenSSL to libsecp256k1, gives first-party numbers: signature validation is 2.5-5.5x faster. The v0.12.0 release notes say validation is over 5x faster on x86_64, and reindex/new-block validation takes less than half the time. No compiler, flags or benchmark harness is stated for the micro figures, so this cannot be A or B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ECDSA signature validation is 2.5-5.5x faster than OpenSSL, depending on platform (PR #6954 description by Pieter Wuille). The Bitcoin Core v0.12.0 release notes say validation is over five times faster on x86_64, with raw reindex and new-block validation taking less than half the previous time. End-to-end examples in the PR comments: IBD with dbcache=3000 took about 3h48m vs about 7h37m on OpenSSL-based master (Xeon E31245), and a reindex to block 380912 with dbcache=8000 took 3.2 h vs 8.0 h. No numeric figure was found for signing or key generation.
corrections.hardware: Only for one end-to-end IBD comparison: Intel Xeon E31245 @ 3.30GHz, 16GB RAM, 7200rpm disk (PR #6954 comment). CPU is unstated for the 2.5-5.5x and >5x micro figures.
corrections.caveats: Speedup figures are first-party, from Bitcoin Core developers (who also wrote libsecp256k1), in a 2015 PR and in release notes. They have no published benchmark harness, compiler or flags, and they compare against 2015-era OpenSSL, not a current OpenSSL. Figures cover verification only. Signing moved to libsecp256k1 in v0.10.0 mainly for constant-time and side-channel reasons, not measured speed. The repo's bench binaries (README Benchmark section) time libsecp256k1 alone and do not compare against OpenSSL. The IBD/reindex timings are whole-node measurements that include non-crypto work.

notes: The record said no numbers existed, but PR #6954 and the v0.12.0 release notes give quantified wins over OpenSSL, so the tier goes D to C and the verdict is confirm.
